name: Learning Alliance: structured pedagogy in Ugandan primary schools (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: the one programme, in Iganga District, Eastern Uganda (2025 Pilot Report p. 2).
summary: Learning Alliance gives primary-school teachers in Iganga District, Eastern Uganda, daily scripted phonics lessons, training and coaching visits every few weeks; in 2025, its first year, it spent about {{row:program_expenses}} on {{row:pupils_2025}} pupils in Primary 1 to 3 in 75 schools. Its own comparison with matched schools found a large gain in reading letter sounds but none yet in reading words; counting the two equally and valuing the gain as later earnings gives about {{result}} years of healthy life per $1,000. The biggest uncertainties are how far a small matched comparison run by the charity can be trusted, whether letter sounds turn into reading, and how much of a learning gain lasts into adult earnings.

rows.label: Effect on correct letter sounds per minute after the 2025 year, against matched schools (SD)

source.title: Learning Alliance, '2025 Pilot Report' (April 2026)
source.page: p. 17, table 'Causal impact of Learning Alliance on EGRA Sounds per Minute (2025 cohort)', columns (3)-(4)

rows.explainer: Early Grade Reading Assessment of 727 pupils in 26 of the February government schools and 26 non-programme government schools in the district matched on enrolment, pupil-teacher ratio, rurality and past exam results (pair fixed effects, standard errors clustered by school, in SDs of the control group): +0.625 SD (SE 0.107) in Primary 1 and +0.586 (SE 0.144) in Primary 2. Pooled by precision, 0.61 (SE 0.086, 95% CI 0.44-0.78). Tested in February 2026, after the year-end break, so it is the gain that was left at the start of the next year, not its peak. Primary 3 pupils (about a third) take the Primary 1-2 effect, since the design can't measure them (p. 13); their uncontrolled gains were as large (p. 15).

rows.label: Effect on correct words per minute after the 2025 year, against matched schools (SD)

source.title: Learning Alliance, '2025 Pilot Report' (April 2026)
source.page: p. 18, table 'Causal impact of Learning Alliance on EGRA Correct Words per Minute (2025 cohort)', columns (3)-(4)

rows.explainer: The same comparison for reading whole words: -0.151 SD (SE 0.102) in Primary 1 and -0.040 (SE 0.125) in Primary 2, neither significant. Pooled by precision, -0.11 (SE 0.079, 95% CI -0.26 to 0.05). The report reads it as decoding not yet turned into word reading after one year; the share of pupils reading no words fell by 10 points in Primary 1 (from 48%) and 20 in Primary 2 (from 27%), p. 20, so the bottom of the distribution moved even where the mean didn't.

rows.label: Weight of letter-sound decoding in overall reading skill
rows.explainer: Judgment 50% (35-65%): the evaluation measured two of the early-grade reading assessment's subtasks, a decoding precursor (letter sounds) and a fluency outcome (words); weighting them equally is the unweighted-index convention Kerwin and Thornton report as a robustness check. Anchor: in their randomised trial of a structured literacy programme in northern Uganda (2019, Table 2) the overall index (principal-components weighted, renormalised) rose as much as the sound subtask (0.638 against 0.647), with word reading at 0.22-0.37 and oral fluency 0.48; here words lag sounds by more. Higher if word reading follows from decoding in later years (the report's reading, and the 2026 midline's fall in non-readers); lower because the same midline says the charity doesn't expect its fluency gains to exceed the comparison schools' at the November 2026 endline (Midline p. 1).

rows.label: Correlation between pupils' letter-sound and word-reading scores
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.6 (0.4-0.8): the two subtasks rise together (across the charity's schools, about 5 more words a minute for every 10 more sounds, Midline p. 9: a between-school pattern, not a pupil-level correlation), but half of Primary 1 pupils read no words at all (Midline p. 1), a floor that weakens the correlation among pupils. Used only to put the weighted mix of two subtask effects in SDs of the combined score.

rows.label: Gain in overall reading skill per pupil-year (SD)
rows.formula: (decoding_weight * spm_effect_sd + (1 - decoding_weight) * wpm_effect_sd) / sqrt(decoding_weight * decoding_weight + (1 - decoding_weight) * (1 - decoding_weight) + (decoding_weight * (1 - decoding_weight) + (1 - decoding_weight) * decoding_weight) * subtask_correlation)
rows.explainer: The two measured subtasks, weighted, in SDs of the two-subtask combined score (the weighted mix divided by its own SD), since the earnings figure is per SD of overall skill. For scale, the randomised northern Uganda trial (Kerwin and Thornton 2019, abstract and Table 2) found 0.64 SD on overall reading for the full programme and 0.13 for its reduced-cost version (cascade training, less support).

rows.label: Adult earnings gain per SD of learning that lasts into working life
rows.explainer: The shared figure for low- and middle-income countries (@education.earnings_gain_per_sd_adult_skills_lmic), read with the share of the gain that lasts so fade-out counts once.

rows.label: Share of the learning gain still there in adult life
rows.explainer: The shared figure (@education.test_gain_persistence_to_adulthood): test-score effects of education programmes fade in the years after them. The gain above was measured after the two-month break, so a little of the fade is already in it.

rows.explainer: The shared figure for primary-age programmes (@education.years_primary_programme_to_work): pupils in Primary 1 to 3 are about 5 to 10 years old.

rows.label: Household members who share the earnings gain
rows.explainer: The shared figure (@givewell_shared.resource_sharing_multiplier), as in every model of later-life income.

rows.label: Gain in ln(consumption) per pupil for a year of the programme, discounted to today
rows.formula: ln(1 + learning_gain_sd * edu_earnings_per_sd * edu_persistence) * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, working_years) * (1 + $discount_rate) ^ (0 - years_until_work) * resource_sharing_multiplier
rows.explainer: ln(1 + learning gain × earnings per SD × share lasting) in each working year, discounted to today from when work starts, shared in the household. A proportional gain, so the level of consumption cancels.

rows.label: Consumption per person in Uganda, survey mean (2021 PPP dollars a year, for reading)
rows.explainer: For reading only: the earnings gain is a share of the children's later consumption, so ln(1 + gain) doesn't depend on its level.

rows.label: Benefits to other people, as a share of the pupils' benefits
rows.explainer: Judgment 3% (0-12%): pupils who read may help siblings and classmates outside Primary 1-3. No measurement, so small and wide.

rows.label: Mortality benefits as a share of consumption benefits
rows.explainer: 0: no study of structured pedagogy measures deaths; the longer-run health benefits of literacy (including for the children's own future children) are counted in unmodelled_benefits_adj instead.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment (internal and external validity), a multiplier
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.7 (0.45-0.95). Against the estimate: schools weren't randomised; the matching uses four school characteristics from district records and drops 9 of 35 sampled schools with no good match; there are only 26 pairs; the analysis was designed after the year, by the charity; Primary 3 pupils, a third, take the Primary 1-2 effect unmeasured. For it: the matched schools showed no baseline reading difference (p. 13 note 2), 98% of invited schools joined so there was little self-selection, and three biases push the estimate down (learning lost over the break, a month more teaching in control schools before testing, pupils new to the treatment classrooms; p. 13). Randomised trials of structured literacy in Uganda (Kerwin and Thornton 2019) found effects of this size and larger, so the direction is credible; small matched designs still tend to overstate.

rows.label: Share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Judgment 95% (85-100%): the effect is already net of matched schools teaching as usual. What isn't is the chance that another structured-pedagogy programme would have reached these schools soon; the report names no other structured-literacy programme in the district's comparison schools, and Uganda's mainstream early-grade teaching relies on whole-word memorisation (report p. 23).

rows.label: Learning Alliance's share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.explainer: Judgment 93% (85-98%): Learning Alliance pays for the lesson-plan books, training and coaching. Government and private-school teachers teach the English phonics lessons in school time (website), so their time is not extra; what others add is teachers' three training days (278 teachers, about 3% of the cost at a teacher's daily pay), district officials' time, and the curriculum's localisation for Uganda by Read for Life, a partner NGO based in Gulu (p. 7; the books themselves are bought in Learning Alliance's cost).

rows.label: Attribution share used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Programme received by the July schools, as a share of a full 2025 year
rows.explainer: Judgment 40% (25-55%), against the dose of the February government schools whose effect is measured (term 1, 2-4 weeks of term 2 after the midline, 0-3 weeks of term 3; pp. 7-8). About two thirds of the 75 schools were government (47, p. 14) and the February panel's pupils were 28.5% private (p. 12), so the 25 July schools were roughly half government, half private (our inference). A July government school had 2-4 weeks of term 2 and 0-3 of term 3 after the 32-day strike (p. 8), about a fifth of the February dose; a July private school taught through term 3 (8-10 weeks) as well, about three fifths. Half and half gives about two fifths. The dose matters: learning slowed sharply when lessons stopped (pp. 3-4), and the 2026 midline finds classes further through the lessons gained more (p. 13).

rows.label: Pupil-years of the programme as measured, per pupil reached
rows.explainer: The measured effect is a full 2025 year in the February schools; the July schools count at their share of it. The February private schools weren't in the comparison; their before-and-after gains were similar to the government schools' (p. 15).

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: Judgment 1 (0.9-1.1): no co-funding of the programme is reported, and no other funder would have paid for this work in these schools without the charity.

rows.label: Years a donation waits before the charity spends it
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.25 years (0-0.75): no balance sheet is published (the fiscal sponsor's return covers all its projects); a young charity spending about its yearly budget holds a few months of it.

rows.label: Years from spending to the pupils' gain
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.25 years (0.1-0.5): spending runs through the school year (February to November) alongside the teaching; the earnings wait is counted from the programme year in years_until_work.

rows.label: Discount for the wait before delivery
rows.explainer: Every wait is discounted at the shared rate, like every future benefit; the gains themselves are counted from delivery.

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: 1, measured: Learning Alliance's own count of the pupils in its schools meets an effect from its own controlled evaluation of the same programme in the same year and district (the matched comparison above).

rows.label: Combined adjustment
rows.formula: evidence_adj * counterfactual_adj * attribution_share * implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * wait_discount * missing_data_adj
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above.

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Judgment +9% (-4% to +25%): literacy's benefits beyond earnings, such as health knowledge and better health for the children's own future children (+8%); teachers keeping the phonics routines with later classes after support ends (+3%); against time taken from other subjects and teachers' extra preparation (-2%).
